column5: AI-powered predictive maintenance for railway infrastructure monitoring
column6: PANTOhealth is a German company founded in 2019, officially established in 2020, by Dr. Mina Kolagar, Dr.-Ing. Farzad Vesali, Amir Bashari, and Morteza Nokhodian. The company specializes in predictive maintenance for electrified railway infrastructures, aiming to improve the safety, reliability, and efficiency of rail transport. The founders' combined expertise in energy systems, train engineering, and product development spurred the creation of the company after they identified a critical need for more advanced maintenance solutions in the railway sector. The company's core offering is an AI-powered platform that combines real-time data from on-train IoT devices with digital twin simulations to forecast potential failures and optimize maintenance schedules. This system uses a patented technique to collect data from pantographs, which differs from rival technologies that typically only monitor the catenary (overhead lines). Hardware, including high-resolution cameras, laser sensors, and point cloud scanners, gathers data on critical parameters like contact wire height, thickness, and positioning. This real-world data is supplemented by synthetic data generated by a simulation engine, creating a robust data pool for training the system's AI algorithms. This allows PANTOhealth to pinpoint the exact location of defects with high precision, an accuracy that is enhanced to below 10 centimeters through a partnership with Swift Navigation's Skylark service. PANTOhealth serves a market that includes national infrastructure managers, local municipalities operating trams and city trains, and railway maintenance service providers. The business model is primarily B2B and SaaS-based, offering customized predictive maintenance plans and a suite of products including a Profiling Suite, a Vibration-Based Monitoring Suite, and a Simulation Panel. The company has engaged in pilot projects with major operators like DB Netz AG and Infrabel. Since its inception, which began with a concept in 2018 involving a cellphone strapped to a pantograph, the company has secured multiple rounds of funding, including a pre-seed round in 2020, grant money in 2021, and a six-digit seed round at the end of 2023 led by SCE Freiraum Ventures and EIT Urban Mobility. column5: A revolutionary biotech company, combining world-leading expertise in synthetic biology and 3D bioprinting
column6: Cellbricks Therapeutics is a preclinical biotechnology firm operating from Berlin and Boston, focused on regenerative medicine. Founded in 2016 as a spin-off from the Technical University of Berlin, the company originated from the doctoral research of Dr. Lutz Kloke, who, along with Alexander Thomas and Tobias Lam, established the firm. The core of the company's platform is a proprietary, light-based 3D-bioprinting technology that assembles human cells and custom biomaterials into functional, implantable tissue grafts designed for clinical use. This technology, which uses light projections instead of extruders, is designed to be a fast and gentle process, enabling the creation of complex, vascularized tissues at an industrial scale. The company's business model revolves around developing and producing these implantable tissue therapeutics to address limitations in current cell therapies. Initially, Cellbricks supplied complex in-vitro organ tissues to pharmaceutical companies and research organizations for drug testing and biomedical research. Now, the company is advancing its own therapeutic pipeline. Its primary clients are in the healthcare and pharmaceutical sectors, and it operates in the global regenerative medicine and wound care markets. Revenue is generated through the sale of its bioprinters, such as a unit sold to its clinical manufacturing partner Charité for approximately €50,000, and through the development of its therapeutic products. The company has secured approximately €10 million in funding from investors including ACT Venture Partners, B.Value, and Brooks Hill Partners. Cellbricks is currently pursuing two main therapeutic programs: one for soft tissue reconstruction to treat deep wounds and another for developing implantable liver tissue. The wound healing product, which is its most advanced, uses a patient's own cells to create an autologous fat tissue graft. In April 2025, the company announced successful preclinical results in mice, where the bioprinted grafts demonstrated full integration with host tissue, blood vessel formation, and no signs of rejection or fibrosis after seven weeks. The company's technology platform integrates AI-driven software for designing tissue blueprints and controlling the manufacturing process, ensuring precision and scalability. A key milestone was the company's expansion into the United States in November 2024 with a subsidiary in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and its acceptance into MIT's 'The Engine' accelerator program. Cellbricks plans to advance to pig studies before aiming for human trials by 2027. column5: Self-delivering siRNA drugs for difficult-to-treat diseases
column6: Pramo Molecular GmbH is a German biotechnology company founded in 2021 by Merle Fuchs (CEO), Ida Shaef (CSO), and Thomas Hiller (CTO). The company specializes in developing novel gene silencing therapies for diseases that are currently considered incurable, such as aggressive forms of lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, and heart failure. The core of Pramo Molecular's work is its proprietary platform technology for creating "self-delivering" small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). This technology uses covalently linked, lipid-based molecules to transport nucleic acid-based drugs directly into target cells within organs like the lungs, heart, and pancreas. This approach is a significant development because conventional siRNA delivery has been largely limited to the liver. By enabling efficient downregulation of specific disease-causing proteins in other organs, Pramo addresses a major medical need. Their method avoids the need for nanoparticle packaging and aims to develop new drug candidates at a fraction of the traditional time and cost by using AI, rational drug design, and automated synthesis. The business model is centered on the development and commercialization of its proprietary siRNA therapies. Pramo Molecular develops its own drug candidates while also offering its delivery technology for co-development and licensing to other pharmaceutical companies for specific applications. The company's initial drug candidates target non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Supported by funding from the European Union, the Berlin-based startup is preparing to enter clinical trials. column6: Nano-Join GmbH operates as a specialized materials science company focused on the development and production of advanced sintering pastes. Established in 2015 as a spin-off from the Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin), the firm addresses the increasing demands in the power electronics, automotive, and renewable energy sectors. The company was founded by Gunnar Schulze and Battist Rabay, and is currently led by CEO Dr. Battist Rábay and CTO Dr. Adrian Stelzer, who was appointed as the second managing director in September 2017. The leadership team possesses extensive experience in the development and manufacturing of sintering pastes. The core of Nano-Join's business is providing nanotechnology-based joining solutions that serve as an alternative to traditional solder paste. Its silver and copper sinter pastes are engineered for applications requiring high thermal and electrical conductivity, superior reliability, and robust mechanical strength. These materials are crucial for the performance of high-power electronic components, particularly with the rise of SiC and GaN semiconductors which operate at higher power levels. The client base includes companies in power electronics, optoelectronics, e-mobility, and renewable energy conversion. Revenue is generated through the sale of its standardized paste products and customized R&D projects. The business model received a significant endorsement in November 2024 through a licensing agreement with Inventec Performance Chemicals, which will manufacture and commercialize Nano-Join's technology globally under its ECOREL™ SINTEC product line. Nano-Join's product portfolio centers on silver sintering pastes that offer significant performance advantages, such as thermal conductivity exceeding 250 W/mK and low electrical resistance. A key feature is the ability to achieve strong, long-term stable interconnections at process temperatures well below the classical melting point of the constituent material. The product line includes pastes for various application methods like printing and dispensing, and formulations for both pressure-less and pressure-assisted sintering processes. Notably, their NJ-One paste is solvent-free and stable at room temperature, simplifying storage and handling. These pastes can be applied to diverse surfaces including gold, silver, copper, and nickel. The company has secured funding from investors such as b. value AG and IBB Ventures to scale production and expand internationally. column6: Visseiro GmbH, a Berlin-based startup founded in the autumn of 2018, is focused on transforming elder care through proactive health monitoring. The company was established by Pirmin Kelbel and Janek Jurasch, who, after completing their studies at the Rheinisch-Westfälische Technische Hochschule Aachen (RWTH), relocated to Berlin to launch their venture. Their goal is to create medical technology that integrates seamlessly into daily life, addressing the challenge of adherence to health monitoring systems. The core of Visseiro's offering is a cloud-based sensor system designed for contactless, long-term monitoring of vital signs such as heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiration. This technology is embedded into products like seat cushions and mattresses, allowing for the continuous collection of health data without disrupting the user's daily routine or comfort. The sensors can function through normal clothing, eliminating the need for direct skin contact, a distinct advantage over traditional methods like EKG or pulse oximeters. The collected data is then analyzed by the system's software, which uses AI to detect acute events and long-term health trends, enabling timely interventions. Visseiro primarily serves the geriatric care market, targeting nursing homes, home care services, physicians, and the relatives of elderly individuals. The business model appears to be centered on B2C and B2B sales of their smart sensor products. By providing real-time health data to caregivers and medical professionals, Visseiro aims to mitigate risks such as falls and strokes, thereby enhancing safety and enabling older adults to live independently for longer. In addition to its sensor technology, the company is involved in a research project funded by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) to explore the use of Virtual Reality (VR) in combating social isolation among the elderly. column6: ConBotics GmbH is a Berlin-based robotics developer targeting the construction industry's skilled labor shortage through automation. The company was founded in 2020 by Cristian Amaya, David Franke, and Philipp Heyne, three engineering graduates from the Technical University of Berlin with experience at the Fraunhofer Institute. Their work on what they termed the "painter's third arm" began in 2020, supported by grants such as the Berlin Startup Grant and the EXIST Business Start-up Grant.  The company's business model centers on providing automated tools to relieve trade professionals from monotonous and physically demanding tasks. ConBotics primarily targets large painting companies that undertake significant projects, offering its main product, the MalerRoboter, through a rental model to avoid high acquisition costs for its clients. A sales model is planned for 2025. The company generates revenue by renting its robotic solutions, which are distributed through established sales partners in the industry.  ConBotics' flagship product is the MalerRoboter, an autonomous robot for interior surface coating. It is marketed as the world's lightest painting robot, weighing 130 kg in total, with its heaviest component being a 60 kg mobile platform. The system consists of a self-developed, patented lightweight robot arm mounted on a mobile, autonomous platform that also carries a paint sprayer, a 35-liter paint container, and a battery. Using AI, the robot navigates spaces, identifies obstacles like windows and doors, and follows walls to apply paint with a spray gun. This allows it to handle large, monotonous surfaces, reportedly completing jobs twice as fast as manual labor and reducing personnel requirements by up to 80%. The robot's precision work can also lower paint consumption by up to 20%. While the robot paints, human workers can focus on more complex tasks. ConBotics plans to expand its product line with robotic tools for sanding, floor coating, and applying filler, all utilizing the same universal mobile platform. column5: A company that is engaged in the design, development and commercialization of fluidic devices
column6: FDX Fluid Dynamix GmbH, a Berlin-based deep-tech company, operates in the industrial supplies and parts sector with a B2B manufacturing business model. Founded in May 2015, the company emerged as a spin-off from the Technical University of Berlin, building on a research project that received significant initial funding. The founding team consists of three engineers, Dr.-Ing. Bernhard Bobusch (CEO), Dr.-Ing. Oliver Krüger (CTO), and Dr.-Ing. Jens Wintering (CPO), who met during their studies and possess extensive experience in combustion, fluid mechanics, and production engineering. Their academic and research backgrounds are directly applied to the company's core technology. FDX centers its operations on its patented OsciJet nozzle technology, which is based on the principle of fluidic oscillators. These nozzles create a self-induced, high-frequency oscillating or pulsating fluid jet without any moving parts, making them exceptionally robust and wear-free. This design addresses a core challenge in many industrial processes by introducing dynamic fluid flows that improve efficiency. The company's business model involves the design, development, commercialization, and manufacturing of these fluidic devices, offering both a standard product portfolio and custom-tailored solutions from a database of over 6,000 nozzle designs. FDX serves a wide range of industries including automotive, process engineering, and agriculture. Applications are diverse, ranging from high-pressure cleaning and fuel injection for gas turbines to mixing systems for the pharmaceutical and biotech industries. For instance, their nozzles have been used in car washes to reduce water consumption and in food production for hygienic cleaning of equipment. The primary product, the OsciJet nozzle, offers distinct advantages depending on its application, such as enhanced cleaning, superior mixing, improved cooling, and broader spray distribution. The oscillation frequency can be tuned from a few hertz to ultrasonic values, which allows for up to 15 times better mixing and 7 times more effective cleaning compared to conventional nozzles. Complementing the hardware, FDX developed the OsciNet system, a monitoring solution that transforms the OsciJet into a "Nozzle 4.0". OsciNet uses sensors to measure the nozzle's oscillation frequency, which directly correlates to the flow rate, enabling real-time monitoring, malfunction detection, and automated documentation of resource consumption. column6: Reachtag GmbH, operating as Reachtag, was a Berlin-based startup founded in 2019 by Benjamin Gareis and Ege Aksungur. The founders, who had previously experienced losing personal items, established the company after identifying a gap in the market for an affordable and straightforward loss prevention solution. The venture originated at the Technical University of Berlin, supported by the Berliner Startup Stipendium, and later received an undisclosed amount in a grant prize from the university in June 2019. This was achieved through a system of physical tags, such as reachtag KEY, reachtag THINGS, and reachtag PHONE, which could be attached to various personal belongings. The technology allowed for communication via a simple phone call without revealing the owner's private data, including their telephone number, even during a callback. This focus on privacy and the low price point were the service's primary differentiators. The business model was described as a B2B platform, suggesting it may have targeted other businesses as clients, and operated on a subscription basis, costing a few cents a month. Reachtag's product lineup included tags for keys, general items, and phones, and later expanded to include reachtag CAR, which allowed drivers to be contacted anonymously. The system aimed to provide a faster and more direct alternative to traditional lost and found offices. Despite initial plans for launching new digital products and expanding its retail presence, the company was shut down and entered liquidation in 2022. column6: Based in Berlin, Diaven, operating under the brand Labfly, is a medical drone delivery service provider established in 2018 by a group of engineers during their college years. Their primary clients include hospitals, pharmacies, research institutions, and governmental bodies involved in healthcare. Diaven operates in the urban air mobility (UAM) market, which is projected to expand significantly as cities seek to alleviate road congestion and reduce carbon emissions. The company's business model centers on providing a specialized drone delivery service. Diaven has developed its own proprietary drone, the Labfly 1000, which is specifically engineered for healthcare logistics. The drone features a 6-liter insulated payload compartment made of foam and fiberglass, capable of carrying up to 1 kg. Redundancy is a core design principle, with the drone equipped with eight propulsion systems (double the required four) and a dual-battery backup, ensuring it can complete its journey even with multiple system failures. For emergencies, an integrated parachute can be deployed automatically or manually. The Labfly 1000 is available in two models: a top-loading version that lands for delivery and a bottom-loading variant that can drop payloads without landing. Beyond its delivery services, Diaven also offers its expertise in custom drone design, software solutions, and other drone applications to address various logistical challenges. column6: Sicoya GmbH is a semiconductor company specializing in silicon photonics-based solutions for optical data interconnects. The firm was established in January 2015 as a spin-off from the Technical University of Berlin, building upon research and development in silicon photonics that began in 2007. Its founding team includes Sven Otte (CEO), Stefan Meister (CTO), Hanjo Rhee, Christoph Theiss, and Marco Vitali.  The company's core business involves the development, manufacturing, and sale of highly integrated silicon photonic chips, optoelectronic devices, and optical modules. Sicoya's key technological differentiator is a monolithic integration process that combines analog electronics and optical components on a single silicon chip. This approach significantly reduces power consumption, manufacturing costs, and the physical size of interconnects while increasing data transmission rates. The company operates on a fabless business model, focusing on the design and sale of Application-Specific Photonic Integrated Circuits (ASPICs) while outsourcing the manufacturing process. Its product portfolio serves optical transceiver vendors and system vendors, offering solutions like 100G, 400G, and 800G transceivers designed for intra-data center connections and 5G wireless applications.  In November 2015, Sicoya secured €3.5 million in a Series A funding round led by Target Partners to advance product development. A significant milestone occurred in October 2021, when Suzhou Dawning Semi Technology Co., Ltd. (DAWNSEMI) completed a 100% acquisition of Sicoya. Following the acquisition, Sicoya and its parent company announced plans to establish a global R&D center and product manufacturing base, including a packaging factory in Tianjin, China, to serve the local market and scale production. column6: AST - Advanced Sailing Technologies GmbH, a German boat-building company, was founded in the summer of 2017 by Thilo Keller and Catarina Jentzsch. The founders' journey originated from a shared passion for competitive sailing and a deep technical background. Thilo Keller, a naval architect specializing in hydrodynamics and yacht design, has been an active A-Class catamaran racer for nearly two decades, securing 20 international titles. His experience led him to invent the ACC – Automatic Cant Control, a pioneering stable foil system for A-Class catamarans. Keller and Jentzsch met during a university sailing regatta and collaborated on a project to build a solid wing for an A-Class catamaran. After gaining industry experience post-graduation, they established AST to focus on building high-performance boats and lightweight composite parts.The company's business model centers on the design, manufacture, and sale of high-performance watercraft, specifically targeting the recreational sailing and luxury tender markets. Revenue is generated through the direct sale of their boats. A key aspect of their manufacturing philosophy is the industrialization of boat building in Germany, ensuring quality and durability. The firm operates from a modern shipyard with advanced insulation and dust and chemical filtering systems. Their production process emphasizes sustainability, utilizing a closed-mould process for composite parts to minimize emissions and using recycled materials, such as PET foam cores made from plastic bottles.AST's product line began with "The Foiling Dinghy," a single-handed dinghy featuring a foil system derived from A-Class racing, which sold 120 boats in its first two years. These tenders are designed to be lighter and 35% more power-efficient than traditional RIBs, making them suitable for electric propulsion. column6: Panono, operating under Professional360 GmbH, is a Berlin-based company specializing in high-resolution 360-degree imaging technology. The company's journey began with its founding in October 2012 by Jonas Pfeil, Björn Bollensdorff, and Qian Qin. The concept originated from Pfeil's master's thesis in computer engineering at the Technical University of Berlin. The firm gained significant traction through highly successful crowdfunding campaigns on Indiegogo and Companisto, raising approximately $1.25 million and €1.6 million, respectively. The core offering is the Panono Camera, a distinctive grapefruit-sized spherical device equipped with 36 individual camera modules. When triggered, these cameras simultaneously capture images that are then uploaded to Panono's cloud platform for automatic stitching. This process produces a single, high-resolution 108-megapixel, fully spherical panoramic image with no blind spots. The camera's design, which avoids wide-angle lenses, minimizes the distortion commonly found in other 360-degree cameras. The camera features 16GB of internal storage, capable of holding around 600 panoramic shots, and is controlled via a dedicated mobile app for iOS and Android. This app allows users to remotely trigger the camera, preview images, and manage cloud uploads. The business model combines hardware sales with a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) component for its cloud-based image processing and hosting services, which also enables monetization for content providers. Primarily targeting the B2B sector, Panono's technology serves professional clients who require high-quality panoramic content for various applications. Despite its promising start, Panono GmbH filed for insolvency proceedings in May 2017. Subsequently, the company's assets, trademarks, and patents were acquired by Bryanston Group AG, a Swiss private equity firm, and business operations were restarted under a new holding company, Professional360 GmbH. column5: A Berlin start-up in the field of medical technology
column6: Remod is a Berlin-based medical technology company focused on rehabilitation for patients with posture and movement control deficits, primarily those resulting from central nervous system disorders. The company’s history is deeply rooted in the personal experience of its founders, the mother-daughter team of Anna Vonnemann and Dindia Gutmann. Dindia Gutmann has had spastic hemiparesis, a partial paralysis of one side of the body, since birth due to a stroke. Faced with a lack of effective long-term aids, the pair developed their own device, creating the first prototype in 2005. This foundational experience led to the establishment of Remod UG. Anna Vonnemann, a biologist, serves as CEO and is the patent holder, while Dindia Gutmann, who studied economics, provides crucial insights as the primary idea generator and long-term user. The company operates within the rehabilitation technology market, serving patients with conditions like hemiparesis, stroke, infantile cerebral palsy, and multiple sclerosis who are still able to walk. Its business model appears to revolve around the direct sale of its medical devices and accompanying therapy concepts to patients and therapists. The company has also utilized crowdfunding to finance specific projects, such as a training book. Remod's core products are the ReMoD V5 and GT1 orthoses, wearable biofeedback devices designed as vests. These are classified as medical devices that meet EU regulations. The system works by detecting deviations from a pre-set ideal posture and then sending electro-tactile signals to the user's skin in real-time. This process provides artificial sensory feedback, helping patients perceive their body's position and movement, information that is often impaired by their condition. The goal is to enable patients to independently correct their posture and (re)learn a more symmetrical gait, which can prevent secondary damage like joint pain and muscle regression. The devices are designed to be simple, with just three buttons for operation. The company has received significant support, including an EXIST grant, funding from the EU's Horizon 2020 program, and investments from Carsten Maschmeyer and Dagmar Wöhrl. column5: Simplifying research communication and introducing new ways of collaboration through in-document discussions
column6: PaperHive was a Berlin-based startup founded in 2015 by Dr. André Gaul and Alexander Naydenov. The company aimed to transform the process of reading academic literature from a solitary activity into a collaborative one. Dr. Gaul, a mathematician and computer scientist, brought full-stack development expertise, while Naydenov, with a background in economics and computer science, handled business development and marketing. Their combined experience, including Naydenov's passion for edtech and co-founding a social entrepreneurship incubator, shaped PaperHive's mission. The venture was part of the startup incubator at the Centre for Entrepreneurship at TU Berlin starting in June 2015.  The core of PaperHive's offering was a web platform and browser extension that functioned as a coworking hub for researchers. It allowed users to discuss and annotate research papers directly in the browser, attaching questions, corrections, figures, and code to the text. This created a layer of real-time, contextual discussion on top of publications. The platform served researchers, students, and academic publishers, aiming to improve scientific communication. Key features included collaborative reading, personal literature management in 'Hives,' and tools for post-publication peer review. column6: TissUse GmbH is a German biotechnology firm operating at the forefront of microphysiological systems. Founded in 2010 as a spin-off from the Technische Universität Berlin, the company is commercializing a sophisticated "Multi-Organ-Chip" platform. The scientific founder, Dr. Uwe Marx, is a physician and a serial entrepreneur in the biotech space, having previously co-founded ProBioGen AG and VITA 34 AG. His extensive background in tissue engineering and immunology directly underpins the company's core technology. He led the company as CEO until 2020 before transitioning to the role of Chief Scientific Officer to focus on future innovations. Dr. Reyk Horland, who has been with the company since its inception and holds a Ph.D. in Biotechnology, now serves as CEO, driving the company's commercial growth and strategic partnerships. The company's business revolves around its proprietary and patent-protected HUMIMIC® platform, which emulates human biology on a miniaturized scale. TissUse sells these multi-organ-chip devices, accessories, and offers service contracts to a diverse client base that includes pharmaceutical, chemical, and cosmetic companies. These clients utilize the platform for preclinical assessment of drugs and chemicals, aiming to gain more accurate data on toxicity, absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) profiles, and efficacy. By providing a human-relevant systemic model, TissUse directly addresses the shortcomings of traditional animal testing and static in-vitro cell cultures, offering a solution to reduce and replace animal experiments while potentially streamlining clinical trials. The HUMIMIC® platform is a microfluidic device, the size of a standard microscope slide, capable of culturing miniaturized, three-dimensional organ tissues interconnected by a vascular-like circuit. An on-chip micropump circulates the culture medium, simulating blood flow and enabling organ-to-organ interaction for up to several weeks. This technology allows for the creation of various two, three, and four-organ systems, such as combining intestine, liver, and kidney models to study the metabolic pathway of a substance. The platform is designed for flexibility, compatible with various cell sources including cell lines, primary cells, biopsies, and iPSCs, and works with standard laboratory equipment. Since launching its first products, TissUse has engaged in numerous collaborations with major industry players like AstraZeneca, Bayer, and Roche to develop specific assays for drug development and safety assessment.
